title: Protein Language Modeling 101
content: How does a machine learning model understand the language of proteins? The process isn't so different from the AI chat tools we've all quickly become familiar with. Here’s how what works for words also works for amino acids. Whether or not you work with AI tools day-to-day, you’re probably familiar with the most basic principle of how large language models like Claude or Gemini work. The large language models [LLMs] that power these tools learn patterns in vast datasets of natural language and use those patterns to predict words based on their surrounding context. Protein language models [PLMs] that underlie AI-based protein engineering work much the same way. While the evolutionary, structural, and functional relationships that govern protein sequences are more complex than linguistic grammar, a PLM can learn them just as an AI assistant can learn English or French. Through their understanding of patterns across known sequences, protein language models can predict which mutations are likely to be compatible with a protein’s structure and function. In this article, we’ll explain the basics of how PLMs work for the scientists among us who don’t have additional degrees in computer science. Proteins are assembled from a library of 20 canonical amino acids (protein engineers can also incorporate non-canonical ones—more on that later). A protein’s amino acid sequence determines its structure, which in turn determines its function (the sequence, structure, function paradigm ). A single-chain variable fragment (scFv), which is not even one of the longer protein types, has around 240 amino acids, meaning there theoretically exist 20^240 possible combinations. But only a small fraction of possible amino acid sequences are expected to fold into stable, functional proteins. The fraction found in living organisms, including ourselves, is vanishingly small by comparison. Humans, for example, have around 20,000 protein-coding genes, which can give rise to many more distinct protein forms through various processes. Across all the organisms we rely on for food, medicine, materials, fuels, and more, that adds up to a lot of different proteins. This vast workforce has been shaped by evolutionary pressure as it engaged in its wide array of cellular business. But what if we could also bring ingenuity and technology to bear on tweaking existing proteins to improve their function? Or even create new ones altogether, putting proteins to work on biological fails that evolution hasn’t solved for? That is protein engineering . In the last half-century or so, biochemists and molecular biologists have devised ways of repurposing proteins for use in medicine, agriculture, and industry. Initially, this involved simply purifying naturally-occurring proteins for therapeutic uses. Soon scientists moved on to using chemical intuition and thermodynamic principles, and later, computational simulations, to modify a protein’s sequence of amino acids in a targeted way. This made it possible to optimize protein properties, making them more useful, and even to create novel proteins from scratch . More recently, protein engineers have gone further still, incorporating non-canonical amino acids—variants with chemical properties that the standard 20 don’t possess—to build proteins with capabilities that evolution never produced. This work has yielded tremendous advances, such as life-saving vaccines and cancer immunotherapies , as well as industrial enzymes used in biofuel production, agriculture, and other domains. But these methods of protein engineering are clunky. An antibody drug, for example, must perform well on multiple parameters. Fiddling with the sequence to optimize one property can and often does change, in unpredictable ways, the chemical and physical forces that determine protein folding. That can wipe out function gains from the previous round of optimization and turn the process into a game of molecular whack-a-mole. This makes designing proteins for therapeutics and other applications an expensive, time-consuming, high-risk venture. While clinical potency and efficacy are often the biggest hurdles, further fine-tuning of a single drug candidate generally takes 12-36 months and costs $5-$15 million . Many still fail . Some categories of protein therapies do better , but too often, what looks good in the lab falls apart (sometimes literally) in a person. The process starts with a base model pretrained on public sequence databases, typically tens to hundreds of millions of protein sequences, to learn what a natural protein looks like. Pretraining involves repeatedly exposing the model to millions of evolutionarily successful examples while “masking” some parts of the sequences—that is, deliberately hiding them—and letting the model predict what was in the masked positions.
